cues.text: A Restless Search for Truth

Born around the year 100 at Flavia Neapolis in Samaria, in a family of Greek settlers, Justin gives us, in the opening pages of his Dialogue with Trypho , a portrait of a young man who could not rest content with easy answers.

He went, in turn, to a Stoic who taught him nothing of God, to a Peripatetic more concerned with fees than with wisdom, to a Pythagorean who demanded years of preparatory mathematics he had no patience for, and finally to a Platonist, under whom he felt, for a time, that he was drawing near the very vision of God that philosophy had always promised.
We recognize in Justin something of every earnest seeker: a mind unwilling to settle for what is merely convenient, insisting instead on what is true.
It is a restlessness the Church has always honored, for it is the same restlessness that, rightly followed, leads the human heart toward its true home.
An Old Man by the Sea

It was by the seashore, Justin tells us, walking alone in thought, that he met an elderly stranger who gently dismantled his Platonist confidence, showing him that the philosophers, for all their brilliance, had not seen God, and pointing him instead to the Hebrew prophets , who had spoken by a Spirit greater than any human reasoning, and to Christ, in whom their words had found their fulfillment.
Justin later wrote that a fire was kindled in his soul at these words, and that a love of the prophets and of the friends of Christ possessed him.
He had, at last, found the philosophy that alone was "safe and profitable" — not a system to be mastered, but a Person to be received.
The First Christian Philosopher
Justin did not, on becoming a Christian, abandon philosophy; rather, he came to see it fulfilled.

He continued to wear the philosopher's cloak, teaching openly in Rome, convinced that whatever was true in Plato or the Stoics belonged already, by right, to Christ the Logos — the eternal Word and Reason of God, of whom every human mind that has ever grasped a fragment of truth has, without always knowing it, been given a share.

This conviction, that faith need not fear reason nor reason faith, that the light kindled by the true philosophers and the light revealed in Christ come from the same Sun, became Justin's most lasting gift to the Church, a bridge between the wisdom of Athens and the revelation of Jerusalem that later theologians would build upon for centuries.
A Window Into the Early Church

In his First Apology , addressed directly to the Roman emperor, Justin left us something of incalculable value: an eyewitness description of Sunday worship among the earliest Christians — the reading of "the memoirs of the Apostles" and the writings of the prophets, the president's homily, the common prayers, and then the bringing forward of bread and wine and water, over which thanks is given, so that this food, he tells us, is no longer common bread but the Eucharist , the flesh and blood of the incarnate Jesus.

Across nineteen centuries, this witness still speaks to us with startling clarity and freshness, allowing every believer today to recognize, in the Mass that gathers us on Sunday, the very rhythm of prayer that gathered the household of the Church while the ink of the New Testament itself was scarcely dry.
Faithful Unto Death

Justin's outspoken defense of the Faith drew the hostile attention of a rival philosopher, the Cynic Crescens, whose accusations before the Roman prefect Rusticus led to Justin's arrest along with six companions.

The record of their interrogation survives: asked plainly to sacrifice to the gods, Justin answered that no one in his right mind abandons piety for impiety, and, when sentence of death was pronounced, he and his companions went to their execution, we are told, rejoicing, and confessing the name of Christ to the last.
He was beheaded in Rome around the year 165, becoming himself the very argument he had spent his life constructing: that the truth revealed in Christ was worth more than life itself.
A Companion for Every Age
The Church has never ceased to draw on Justin's example.

He shows us that the search for truth, pursued openly and without fear, does not lead away from Christ but toward him; that the philosopher and the martyr are not two different vocations but can be, as they were in Justin, one and the same total gift of self.

In every generation that has had to give an account of the hope that is in it before a skeptical or hostile world, Justin Martyr walks alongside as an elder brother in the faith, still teaching us that reason, rightly used, is never the enemy of belief, but its truest friend.
